presenterNotes: Piecewise functions are a new and often intimidating concept. Start with the simple two-piece linear function and emphasize the process: check the condition, then evaluate.
When graphing, physically draw the two pieces in different colors and explicitly mark open/closed circles. Students often forget the circles.
Step functions are a great real-world connection. Use the karaoke/rental examples and have students explain why the graph looks like stairs.
Connecting absolute value functions to piecewise functions reinforces both topics. Show that the vertex is the split point, and the two linear pieces meet there.
title: Chapter 4.7 — Piecewise Functions

formulaCard.title: Evaluating a Piecewise Function
notes: Check conditions in order; use the first one that is true.
The domain of each piece is given by its condition.

explanation: A [[kw:piecewise function]] is defined by two or more equations, each applying to a specific part of the domain.
To evaluate, first determine which condition the given x-value satisfies, then use the corresponding equation.
Use a closed circle (●) for inequalities with ≤ or ≥; open circle (○) for < or >.
The function can have gaps, jumps, or changes in direction between pieces.
Always check the boundary conditions carefully—an input at a boundary belongs to the piece with the 'equal to' part.

visuals.title: Evaluating f(x) = { x-2, if x≤0; 2x+1, if x>0 }

teacherCues: Write a piecewise function on the board: f(x) = { x-2 if x≤0, 2x+1 if x>0 }. Ask: 'If x=0, which piece do we use? Why?'
Emphasize checking the condition first, then substituting into the correct expression.

discoveryHook.scenario: A piecewise function is like a multi-tool: different rules for different situations. If you're under 12, the movie ticket costs $8; 12 and over, it's $12. The rule depends on the input—just like a piecewise function where the equation you use depends on the x-value.

blocks.title: Evaluating Piecewise Functions

questions.prompt: A piecewise function is defined by two or more equations, each applying to a different part of the ___.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Each piece applies to a different part of the domain.
hints: It's the set of input values.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = { x-2, if x≤0; 2x+1, if x>0 }, evaluate f(-1).
hints: Check: -1 ≤ 0, so use the first piece.

questions.prompt: In the three-piece function above, which piece gives f(10)? What is the value?

examples.title: A – Evaluating at x=0 and x=4
steps: For x=0: condition 0≤0 is true → use x-2. f(0) = 0-2 = -2.
For x=4: condition 4>0 is true → use 2x+1. f(4) = 2(4)+1 = 9.
examples.prompt: Evaluate f(x) = { x-2, if x≤0; 2x+1, if x>0 } at x=0 and x=4.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How did you decide which piece to use for x = -2? Why not the first piece?
examples.title: B – Three-piece function
steps: x=-8: -8 < -2 → first piece, f(-8)=3.
x=0: -2≤0≤5 → second piece, f(0)=2.
x=3: second piece, f(3)=5.
x=5: second piece, f(5)=7.
x=10: 10>5 → third piece, f(10)=40.

examples.title: C – Distance traveled
examples.prompt: A trip's distance d(x) in miles is: d(x) = { 55x, if 0≤x≤2; 65x-20, if 2<x≤5 }. How far in 4 hours?
steps: 4 satisfies 2<4≤5 → use second piece.

confusionCorner.body: If the condition is ≤ or ≥, the boundary value is included. In the example f(x) = { x-2, x≤0; 2x+1, x>0 }, 0 belongs to the first piece (≤). Always check which piece has the 'or equal to' at the boundary.
confusionCorner.title: Boundary points

blocks.title: Graphing and Writing Piecewise Functions

explanation: To graph a piecewise function, graph each piece within its specified domain interval.
Use an [[imp:open circle]] for endpoints that are not included (< or >).
Use a [[imp:closed circle]] for endpoints that are included (≤ or ≥).
The domain is the union of the domains of all pieces. The range is the set of all y-values produced.
To write a piecewise function from a graph, identify the equations of each line or curve and the x-intervals where they apply.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Graph each piece on its domain; use open/closed circles at boundaries} $$
notes: Domain: all x-values covered by the pieces.
Range: read from the y-axis extent of the graph.
formulaCard.title: Graphing a Piecewise Function

questions.feedbackIfWrong: Open circle for endpoints not included (strict inequalities).
questions.prompt: When graphing a piecewise function, use an open circle for endpoints that are ___ included in the interval.

hints: Look at the condition for the second piece.
questions.prompt: In the graph of y = { -x-4, x<0; x, x≥0 }, what type of circle is at (0,0)?

hints: Use the piece that includes x=0 (x≥0).
questions.prompt: For the graph with y = x+3 (x<0) and y = 2x-1 (x≥0), what is the y-value at x=0?

discoveryHook.scenario: Graphing a piecewise function is like drawing two separate lines on the same grid, each with its own start and end points. One line might stop with an open circle, and the other picks up with a closed circle—creating a picture that can have sharp turns or gaps.

teacherCues: Graph y = { -x-4, if x<0; x, if x≥0 } step by step. Show open circle at (0,-4) for the first piece, closed at (0,0) for the second.

examples.title: A – Graphing a two-piece function
examples.prompt: Graph y = { -x-4, if x<0; x, if x≥0 }. Describe domain and range.
steps: First piece: y = -x-4 for x<0. Ray starting at open circle (0,-4) going up left.
Second piece: y = x for x≥0. Ray starting at closed circle (0,0) going up right.
Domain: all real numbers. Range: y > -4 (the lowest point is at the open circle, so -4 is not included).

examples.prompt: A graph shows a line y = x+3 for x<0, and y = 2x-1 for x≥0. Write the piecewise function.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How did you determine the equation for each piece and the domain intervals?
examples.title: B – Writing a piecewise function from a graph
steps: Left piece: line through (-3,0) and (0,3) with slope 1. Equation: y = x+3. Used for x<0 (open circle at (0,3) if strictly less, but here the second piece picks up at 0). Actually graph shows closed at (0,-1) for right piece. So f(x) = { x+3, if x<0; 2x-1, if x≥0 }.

examples.title: C – Graph with constant piece
examples.prompt: Graph y = { x+8, if x<4; 4x-4, if x≥4 }.
steps: First piece: line y = x+8 from left, open circle at (4,12).
Second piece: line y = 4x-4 from (4,12) with closed circle (since x≥4).
Domain: all real numbers. Range: y ≥ 12? Actually first piece goes down to -∞, second piece starts at 12 and goes up. Range: all real numbers.

confusionCorner.title: Open vs. Closed at Boundaries
confusionCorner.body: At a boundary x = a, if one piece has ≤ or ≥ and the other has < or >, there will be a closed circle on the piece that includes the equal sign, and an open circle on the other piece. This can create a jump or a continuous connection.

confusionCorner.title: Interval Overlap
confusionCorner.body: Step functions must define intervals that don't overlap. Use half-open intervals like (0,1], (1,2] to avoid ambiguity. The endpoint with the 'or equal' should be on one side only.

discoveryHook.scenario: Parking garages often charge a flat rate for each hour or part of an hour. The cost jumps up in steps—$2 for the first hour, $4 for up to two hours, etc. These step functions look like staircases when graphed and model many real-world tiered pricing structures.

The graph consists of horizontal segments that look like steps.

formulaCard.title: Step Function (Karaoke Rental)

steps: Split where x-2 = 0 → x = 2.
If x < 2, then x-2 is negative, so |x-2| = -(x-2) = -x+2.
If x ≥ 2, then x-2 is non-negative, so |x-2| = x-2.
Piecewise: y = { -x+2, if x<2; x-2, if x≥2 }.

Piecewise: y = { -2x-6, if x<-3; 2x+6, if x≥-3 }.

C – Holography reference beam

questions.prompt: The absolute value function |x| can be written as a piecewise function with the split at x = ___.
hints: It's where the expression inside changes sign.
For x<-5, the inside is negative, so use -(x+5).

discoveryHook.scenario: The absolute value function is the most famous piecewise function in disguise! For negative inputs, it multiplies by -1 to 'flip' the sign; for non-negative inputs, it leaves them alone. Recognizing this helps you rewrite any absolute value function as a piecewise function and graph it as two linear pieces.

blocks.title: Writing Absolute Value Functions as Piecewise Functions

confusionCorner.title: Sign of a matters
confusionCorner.body: When writing a|x-h|+k as a piecewise, the a multiplies whatever replaces the absolute value. If a is positive, the left piece has negative slope and the right piece has positive slope (V shape). If a is negative, the left piece has positive slope and the right piece has negative slope (inverted V).

formulaCard.title: Absolute Value as Piecewise
notes: Split where the inside equals zero.
Use the negative of the inside for the left piece, the inside itself for the right piece (if a > 0).

explanation: The absolute value function $ f(x) = |x| $ can be written as a piecewise function: $ f(x) = \begin{cases} -x, & x < 0 \\ x, & x \ge 0 \end{cases} $.
Vertex form $ g(x) = a|x-h|+k $ can also be split at $ x = h $.
The split point is where the expression inside the absolute value changes sign ($ x-h = 0 $).
For $ a|x-h|+k $: if $ x-h < 0 $, then $ |x-h| = -(x-h) $; if $ x-h \ge 0 $, then $ |x-h| = x-h $.
This allows you to graph absolute value functions as two lines meeting at the vertex.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint from Graph
steps: Understand: Two linear pieces, split at x=0.
Solve: Left: y=-x (slope -1). Right: y=x (slope 1). Domains: left x<0, right x≥0.
Conclude: f(x) = { -x, if x<0; x, if x≥0 }. This is the absolute value function.
examples.prompt: Graph shows a V-shape with vertex at (0,0), left line y=-x for x<0, right line y=x for x≥0. Use the blueprint to write the piecewise function.

steps: Understand: Step function with 4 pieces (1st hour, 2nd, 3rd, 4th).
Conclude: Write as piecewise function with those constants and intervals.
examples.title: B – Step Function Blueprint
examples.prompt: Parking costs: first hour $3, each additional hour $2, max 4 hours. Use the blueprint.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How does the blueprint help you organize the constant pieces and their intervals?

examples.title: C – From Context to Piecewise
steps: Understand: First mile (0<x≤1) costs $3. After that, each additional mile adds $2.
Conclude: C(x) = { 3, if 0<x≤1; 2x+1, if 1<x≤10 }.
examples.prompt: A taxi charges $3 for the first mile and $2 per mile after that, up to 10 miles. Write the piecewise function for cost C(x) for distance x.

explanation: The blueprint for piecewise functions: [[imp:Understand]] – Look at the graph (or description) and identify how many pieces there are and the x-interval for each piece.
[[imp:Solve]] – For each piece, determine the type of function (linear, constant) and find its equation using the methods from earlier sections.
[[imp:Conclude]] – Write the piecewise function using the standard format, with the equation and its condition. Check endpoints for open/closed circles.

notes: Order doesn't matter, but list from leftmost interval to rightmost.
Use correct inequality symbols with open/closed circles.
formulaCard.title: Piecewise Blueprint

rows.1: Identify pieces: left line, right line. Their domains: x<0 and x≥0.
Left line: y=x+3. Right line: y=2x-1.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Mastering Piecewise Functions

confusionCorner.body: When writing a piecewise function from context, decide whether the boundary belongs to the lower or higher interval. Typically, for step functions, we use (a, b] to avoid overlap. For continuous functions, the boundary is included in one piece and not the other.
confusionCorner.title: Including/Excluding Boundaries

discoveryHook.scenario: Piecewise functions can look complex, but the blueprint breaks them down. Understand the pieces and their intervals, Solve for each piece's equation, and Conclude by putting them together in the standard piecewise notation. It's like assembling a puzzle!

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Use a problem that asks to write a piecewise function from a graph.
Emphasize: 'Understand' identifies the pieces and their domains; 'Solve' writes the equations; 'Conclude' assembles the piecewise function.
